tldr: To solve long-horizon tasks, this new world model quantizes latent states using the time it actually takes for a low-level controller to reach them (first-passage time), directly coupling global discrete search with continuous visual feedback control.
hero_caption: Overall concept of VQ-WM. Latent states extracted from images are discretized based on the controller's regions of attraction (reachability). A macro-level plan is constructed via shortest-path search on a discrete graph, while a continuous visual feedback controller sequentially tracks each intermediate target.
overview:
Visual world models that predict the future from images to decide actions are powerful. However, they easily break down on long-horizon robot tasks that require many steps. When performing multi-step autoregressive rollouts in a continuous latent space, prediction errors compound like a snowball, and the resulting plans often become impossible for low-level controllers to execute.

To solve this, the authors bring the classical idea of feedback motion planning (such as LQR-Trees, which plans motions by taking into account the stabilization regions of controllers) into world models. The result is VQ-WM (Vector-Quantized World Model). Its key innovation lies in how latent states are clustered into discrete representative points (a codebook): instead of conventional Euclidean distance, it uses the first-passage-time (FPT)—the number of control steps a learned controller takes to reach a target—as a quasi-metric.

This builds a discrete state graph made up exclusively of goals the controller can reliably reach and stabilize. A high-level planner can find long-horizon plans spanning several minutes in less than a second simply by running breadth-first search on this graph. Then, the low-level controller sequentially reaches each intermediate node with continuous visual feedback, preventing execution drift from compounding.

In real-robot evaluations on the 4-disk Tower of Hanoi puzzle (requiring at least 15 moves), state-of-the-art VLAs ($\\pi_{0.5}$) and world-action models (Cosmos Policy) failed to compose long-horizon solutions from short play data. In contrast, VQ-WM achieved a 100% task progress rate. In simulations, it also substantially outperformed H-JEPA, one of the strongest prior world models.
contributions: Proposed VQ-WM, a latent feedback motion planning framework that seamlessly integrates discrete long-horizon graph search with continuous visual feedback control.

Introduced First-Passage Time (FPT)—which reflects the controller's reachability—into latent state vector quantization, and developed a framework to estimate it from closed-loop rollouts within a learned world model.
Achieved a 100% success rate on a physical robot 4-disk Tower of Hanoi puzzle by synthesizing and executing optimal 15-move plans without any full-task demonstrations (using only short-play data).

Demonstrated substantial performance gains over existing state-of-the-art world models (such as H-JEPA) by 13.3 to 85.3 percentage points across manipulation and locomotion (Walker) simulation benchmarks.

sections.heading: Why do existing world models fail on long-horizon tasks?
sections.summary: Because vision-based world models make multi-step predictions in continuous spaces, longer horizons lead to compounding prediction errors and search explosion. This paper proposes VQ-WM, which discretizes latent space by considering the regions a controller can stabilize, achieving both long-horizon prediction and reliable tracking.
sections.details:
Visual world models have attracted great interest in robotics because they can predict future states from images and search for optimal action sequences. However, for long-horizon tasks requiring many consecutive steps (such as rearranging blocks in sequence), practical deployment remains extremely difficult.

Most existing methods autoregressively unroll and optimize action sequences step-by-step within continuous latent spaces. As the planning horizon grows, prediction errors compound rapidly, and the search space explodes. Furthermore, even if a plan appears seamless in latent space, there is no guarantee that the robot's real low-level controller can reliably pass through and stabilize around those intermediate states.

Classical robot control theory offers an elegant concept called LQR-Trees, which builds global motion plans by chaining together the regions of attraction (regions where a local feedback controller can recover from errors and pull the system to the goal). This work brings that exact philosophy into modern latent world models.

Specifically, it measures the First-Passage Time (FPT)—the time required for the controller to reach a target—and performs vector quantization (VQ) on the state space based on this metric. It then searches for the shortest path to the goal on the resulting discrete graph and sequentially tracks the planned intermediate goals with a visual feedback controller. This alignment of planning abstraction with controller capabilities is the core of this research.

captions.F1: Conceptual diagram of VQ-WM. Each state code acts as the core of a controller's region of attraction $\mathcal{R}$. The high-level planner searches for paths over the discrete transition graph, and the low-level controller reliably tracks each goal via visual feedback as if passing through funnels.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of world models, abstraction, and feedback control
sections.summary: This work brings together three research lines: visual world models for planning, hierarchical/discrete abstraction for long-horizon tasks, and feedback motion planning. The decisive difference from prior approaches is embedding controller reachability directly into the discretization metric of the latent space.
sections.details:
Related work in this paper can be organized into three main categories.

### II-A World Models for Visual Planning
Methods that learn latent dynamics to optimize policies include Dreamer and TD-MPC, as well as DINO-WM, which plans zero-shot from image goals. However, these rely on continuous action optimization; as horizons grow long, search costs skyrocket, and compounding errors cause plans to fail. VQ-WM avoids full continuous action sequence optimization, replacing it with graph search over discretized states.

### II-B Abstraction for Long-Horizon Planning
Approaches exist that introduce temporal hierarchies like H-JEPA, discretize macro actions like Hi-LeWM, or construct graphs by estimating goal reachability from value functions like SoRB and L3P. However, simply hierarchizing latent space or partitioning it by geometric distance does not guarantee that the generated subgoals are actually easy for the underlying control system to reach. Because VQ-WM quantizes states based on first-passage time from closed-loop rollouts, the planning units are tied directly to the controller's capabilities.

### II-C Feedback Motion Planning and Goal-Conditioned Control
Classical feedback motion planning (such as Burridge et al.'s funnel approach and Tedrake et al.'s LQR-Trees) guides systems to goals by chaining together regions that local controllers can funnel into. While many recent deep learning approaches learn goal-conditioned policies from play data, VQ-WM quantifies reachability via closed-loop simulation inside a learned world model, faithfully reproducing this composition principle in visual latent space.

sections.heading: Problem setup: reaching goal images from offline data
sections.summary: The paper defines a visual control problem where a robot must navigate from an initial image to a goal image using only a reward-free offline trajectory dataset. At test time, it must reach an arbitrary given goal image zero-shot.
sections.details:
This work considers a controlled Markov process with observation space $\mathcal{O}$ and physical action space $\mathcal{A}$. At each time step $t$, the robot receives an observation such as an image $o_t \in \mathcal{O}$ and executes an action $a_t \in \mathcal{A}$.

The input provided is an offline dataset of $N$ trajectories without reward labels: $\mathcal{D} = \{(o_0^{(n)}, a_0^{(n)}, \ldots, a_{T_n-1}^{(n)}, o_{T_n}^{(n)})\}_{n=1}^{N}$. The length of individual episodes $T_n$ can be relatively short.

The objective is to autonomously guide the robot from an initial observation $o_{\mathrm{init}}$ presented at test time to the state indicated by a specified goal image $o_{\mathrm{goal}}$. No reward signals from the environment or task-specific reward functions are used.

sections.heading: Quantization via First-Passage Time (FPT) and two-stage planning
sections.summary: VQ-WM builds a state codebook on top of pretrained visual representations using closed-loop control steps (FPT) as a quasi-metric. At test time, it determines global paths via discrete graph search and tracks them with a low-level visual feedback controller.
sections.details:
### IV-A Overall Architecture
VQ-WM consists of seven main modules: a frozen image encoder $E_Z$ (V-JEPA 2, a self-supervised model, is used here), a continuous state predictor $P_Z$, a goal-conditioned controller $\pi$, state and action quantizers $\phi_Z, \phi_U$, codebooks $\mathcal{Q}, \mathcal{U}$, and a discrete state transition predictor $P_Q$.

The critical insight is to avoid using Euclidean distance for state quantization. States that are geometrically close in latent space can still be difficult for a robot controller to reach. Therefore, the number of controller calls required to reach the neighborhood of a target—the First-Passage Time (FPT)—is defined as an asymmetric quasi-metric $d(z, z')$ and used for quantization.

### IV-B Inference (Planning and Control)
Inference operates via a dual-loop mechanism: a low-frequency planning loop and a high-frequency control loop (Figure F2(a)).

- **Planning loop**: Initial and goal images are converted into latent states $z_{\mathrm{init}}, z_{\mathrm{goal}}$ and quantized into state codes $q_{\mathrm{init}}, q_{\mathrm{goal}}$. Using the discrete dynamics predictor $P_Q(q' \mid q, u)$, it expands the transition graph online and finds the shortest code sequence $(q_0, q_1, \ldots, q_L)$ via breadth-first search (BFS). Computation is extremely fast: a plan equivalent to roughly 5 minutes of robot operation completes in under 1 second on an RTX 5080.
- **Control loop**: Using each planned node $q_i$ sequentially as a target, the controller $a_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid z_t, q_i)$ drives the robot with visual feedback. The allocated steps for each subgoal are determined by the previously estimated FPT.

### IV-C Training Pipeline
Training proceeds through the following steps (Figure F2(b)):

1. **Training controller and continuous predictor**: Pairs with time offsets $r \in \{0, \ldots, R\}$ are sampled from offline trajectories to train the goal-conditioned policy $\pi$ and continuous predictor $P_Z$ using multi-step closed-loop rollout loss.
2. **Building the state codebook**: Closed-loop simulations of predictor $P_Z$ and policy $\pi$ are run to estimate the FPT $d(z, z')$ between state pairs in the dataset. Regions reachable within $R$ steps are treated as regions of attraction $\hat{\mathcal{R}}$, and a minimal set of representative points covering all data points is extracted using a greedy set cover algorithm to form codebook $\mathcal{Q}$.
3. **Learning discrete latent dynamics**: From pairs $(q_t, q_{t'})$ where states change, the latent action encoder $E_U$, action codebook $\mathcal{U}$, and transition predictor $P_Q$ (which outputs categorical distributions) are trained simultaneously.

captions.F2: Overall pipeline of VQ-WM. (a) At inference, discrete graph search (slow) sets global subgoal sequences, and controller $\pi$ executes them via visual feedback (fast). (b) In offline training, FPT is computed from $\pi$ and $P_Z$ rollouts, greedy set cover determines the state codebook $\mathcal{Q}$, and the discrete transition model $P_Q$ is trained.

sections.heading: 100% success on real Tower of Hanoi! Pushing past world model limits
sections.summary: Evaluations on a real robot arm solving Tower of Hanoi and several simulation benchmarks showed that VQ-WM autonomously synthesizes 15-move plans from short play data alone, demonstrating robustness that far exceeds current VLAs and world models.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated three aspects: partial trajectory composition capability, long-horizon execution stability, and the advantages of FPT quantization.

### V-A Simulation Benchmarks
Evaluations were conducted on the Stable-WorldModel Cube (cube manipulation) and Scene (compound multi-object manipulation) environments across three settings: Cube-Easy (25 steps ahead), Cube-Hard (pick-and-place over 20-step segments), and Scene (sequentially manipulating buttons, drawers, windows, etc., 50 steps ahead).

VQ-WM achieved the highest success rate across all environments, outperforming the best baselines by +8.0 points in Cube-Easy, +13.3 points in Cube-Hard, and +28.0 points in Scene. While Temporal Straightening (which forces the latent space to flatten) struggled at 10.7% on Cube-Hard, VQ-WM reached 73.3%. It also beat H-JEPA, the strongest world model baseline, by 13.3 points on Cube-Hard because it avoids generating unreachable subgoals.

In a locomotion task (Walker), performance jumped from 12–22% with image observations alone to 97.3% simply by adding proprioceptive inputs (joint angles, etc.) to the controller, without changing the planner structure at all (DINO-WM stayed at 12.0% even with proprioception). This demonstrates how improvements in controller capability are directly reflected in reachable sets.

### V-B Physical Robot Experiment: Tower of Hanoi
A WidowX robot arm was evaluated on a physical puzzle transferring 4 disks to another peg (Figure F3). The optimal solution requires 15 moves (H15), demanding over 5 minutes of continuous high-precision grasping, aligning, and inserting.

- **Expert data setting**: On 1-move tasks (H1), Cosmos Policy (WAM) and $\pi_{0.5}$ (VLA) both achieved 100%. But on the 15-move H15, compounding errors caused their success rates to drop sharply to 76% and 23%, respectively. V-JEPA 2-AC, which searches over continuous actions, scored 0% (reaching 94% only when manually provided 6 subgoal images). In contrast, VQ-WM achieved a **99.6%** task progress rate.
- **Non-expert (short play data) setting**: In this rigorous setting, the model had to solve the full 15-move task using play data containing at most 5 moves per trajectory. Cosmos Policy scored 5% and $\pi_{0.5}$ scored 3%, failing almost completely. VQ-WM achieved a **100%** progress rate, proving it can freely compose novel long-horizon solutions from local trajectories.

### V-C State Quantization Ablation Study
In a simulated Tower of Hanoi, the authors compared building the codebook with standard squared Euclidean distance versus FPT. While Euclidean distance peaked at around 40% success, FPT achieved around 90% (a +50 percentage point gap). Performance remained stable across a wide codebook size range of 250 to 2000, confirming that FPT synchronizes effectively with controller execution capabilities.

captions.F3: Real robot arm (WidowX) solving the 4-disk Tower of Hanoi puzzle. Starting from the initial state, it completes 15 precise disk transfers to rebuild the stack perfectly on the target peg.

sections.heading: Looking ahead: replanning frequency and multi-task scaling
sections.summary: While open-loop planning once per episode was used to evaluate the framework's baseline stability, future work includes exploring MPC-style high-frequency replanning and scaling to multi-task foundation models.
sections.details:
The authors highlight two main limitations and future directions.

First, **leveraging replanning**. Because VQ-WM's discrete search is fast (under 1 second), it is theoretically possible to update global plans every step or every few seconds like Model Predictive Control (MPC). However, to evaluate tracking stability under pure feedback motion planning, current experiments used open-loop search planned once at episode start. Investigating the tradeoffs between computational cost and the benefits of frequent replanning, such as recovering from large unexpected disturbances, remains open for study.

Second, **scaling to multi-task, general-purpose settings**. The modular nature of this method makes it straightforward to replace the state encoder with a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) and use a multi-task policy as the controller. Even if the controller changes, FPT-based state quantization can adapt without rewriting the planner's algorithm, offering an appealing path toward diverse everyday manipulation tasks.

sections.heading: Takeaway: controller-aware abstraction unlocks long-horizon visual planning
sections.summary: VQ-WM significantly stabilizes long-horizon manipulation with world models by combining FPT-based discretization with discrete search and continuous feedback control.
sections.details:
This paper introduced VQ-WM, a latent feedback motion planning framework that merges discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control.

The core bottleneck in long-horizon planning with world models has been whether the low-level controller can actually achieve the intermediate targets set by the high-level planner. By establishing First-Passage Time (FPT) under learned closed-loop dynamics as the quantization criterion, this work aligns the planner's discrete graph directly with controller capabilities.

The strong results on the physical Tower of Hanoi and simulation benchmarks show that the classical principle of controller-dependent state abstraction remains an effective guide in the era of deep world models.

takeaways: Replacing geometric Euclidean distance in latent space with First-Passage Time (FPT)—the time a controller takes to reach a target—prevents the generation of unreachable goals.

Dividing labor between low-frequency discrete graph search for global planning and high-frequency continuous visual feedback for local execution mitigates compounding errors and boosts efficiency (planning a 5-minute task in under 1 second).

Even with only short play data (partial trajectories), building a state graph based on controller regions of attraction enables zero-shot execution of unseen, ultra-long-horizon tasks like 15-move puzzles.
limitations: To demonstrate the baseline stability of the search framework, planning was done open-loop once per episode, leaving real-time replanning (MPC) in dynamic environments unverified.
Estimating first-passage time requires running numerous closed-loop rollouts on a world model learned from offline data, leading to relatively heavy upfront computation when building the codebook.
Evaluations focused primarily on single tasks and limited domains; scaling to open-world, large-scale multi-task settings with language instructions remains future work.
